message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/<area>-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999 via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session) ; `alloc_id()` for element ids (from `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case, from the catalog), snapshots the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (which calls every module's `check(pr)`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step labelled by the command's catalog label (`always_step` hooks force a step even when nothing changed).
- `src/commands/mod.rs` (dispatch: each module's `dispatch(s, cid, p)` is tried in turn), `src/commands/basic.rs` (new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid; `open_path`, `write_atomic`), `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers producing the original's texts: `` `x` in mm is required``, ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9), `src/model.rs` (levels by elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` with the original's errors, `find` by id/GUID, `normalize_guid`), `src/check.rs` (core rules: level/grid; your rules go in your module's `check`).
- Done by others (reuse, don't redo): `src/rvt/` (Revit import; `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a planar-faces tracer and `src/rvt/rooms.rs` a room-enclosure test), `src/cloud/` (point clouds), `src/deflate.rs` (zlib/deflate byte-identical to the original's flate2: `zlib_compress` fast, `zlib_compress_level`), `src/inflate.rs`, `src/util.rs` (base64, fnv1a64), `src/media/` (pictures, `material`, `favorite`, `library`, `paint`), `src/styles/` (line/fill patterns, line styles, region/text/dimension types, line weights, object styles, units, room_area, language, standard, phase, phase_filter, option, parameter, voltage, distribution_system, wire_type, reinforcement_preset; `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` give new/copied elements their phase/option params; `styles::parameters::key_of` for project parameter keys), `src/mcp/`.
- Being written in parallel by others (don't implement these; if you need one, write a minimal private stand-in inside your area and note it): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors, ceilings, shafts, roofs, dormers, rooms, room separators, stairs, ramps, railings, masses and by-face, sketch/edit_boundary/edit_shape/add_point/add_split_line/reset_shape/falls, flip, show_mass; `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`), STRUCTURE (column, structural_column, footing, beam, strip_footing, pipe, duct, conduit, cable_tray, wire, down_conductor, ground_conductor, cabling, rebar, reinforce, type, family, symbol_set, component, the sizing calculators; `src/structure/`), VIEWS (sections, elevations, sheets, place, crop, duplicate_view, scale, detail, visual_style, graphics, filter, template, section_box, perspective, graphic_display_options, camera, work_plane, text, dimension*, tag, spot, spot_slope, detail_line and its join/explode/vertex/convert_spline/offset/trim_extend, filled_region, groups, linework, make_fill_pattern; `src/views/`), EDIT (modify, move, copy, rotate, mirror, corner, split, fillet, align, match_properties, delete, insert, link, reload, purge, delete_type, rename_type, autosave, recover; `src/edit/`), READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, measure, select_by_id, ids_of, filter_selection, and the project-file loader `src/load.rs`; `src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`), IFC-EXPORT (`src/ifc/export*`), IFC-IMPORT (`src/ifc/import*`). Rendering (render, PNG/SVG/PDF/GLB), CAD/DXF, the sample house and the highrise come later.

## How to test
`MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels exactly. Useful trick: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`) and run both programs on that file — the loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params` text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases, every error and the order of checks). Learn element formats from the original's saved files.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't; edits outside your area; what other areas must provide or call.

## YOUR AREA: STRUCTURE (`src/structure/`)
Commands: `column`, `structural_column`, `footing`, `beam`, `strip_footing`, `pipe`, `duct`, `conduit`, `cable_tray`, `wire`, `down_conductor`, `ground_conductor`, `cabling` (runs: justification, offsets, end_offset, risers, systems, closed chains, type sections), `rebar`, `reinforce` (beams, columns incl. round, footings, floors incl. sloped and with openings — floors and walls are ARCH's, so create floors by writing the JSON the original saves, or by loading original-made projects; the `check` "NBR 6118" notes, presets via `styles::presets::find`), `type` (Edit Type for every category in its spec, including wall/floor/roof/ceiling layers and the default type each category uses), `family` (create, change, list, read with types' values worked out and warnings, dry_run, form/symbol patches, delete, path load, save, connectors, operation, kind), `symbol_set` (AREI: 76 families in three languages — observe them all from the original's saved output), `component`, and the calculators `circuit`, `conduit_fill`, `drain_size`, `vent_size`, `hydrant_size`, `load_points` (reads the model's rooms when no `rooms` — rooms are ARCH's; with a private stand-in measure inside walls' finish), `water_size`, `storm_size` (pure functions of their parameters: match every number and error over wide sweeps). Plus the model rules for your categories (in your `check`), and the family formula engine (`Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, + - * / ^, comparisons, if/and/or/not/min/max/abs/sqrt/round/roundup/rounddown/sin/cos/tan in degrees, units of lengths) as a reusable `pub` module (doors/windows of families and IFC export need it). The default project already holds families and types (`/workspace/executable run --save x.bimcraft` shows them); the test assets `/workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/{structure,mep,devices,furniture}.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_structure_elements/structure.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_structure_reinforce/rebar.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_mep_runs/mep.ifc` show which scenarios matter (the IFC export itself isn't yours, but the projects behind those files must come out identical). The MEDIA agent noted: loading a family from favorites must re-allocate fresh ids/GUIDs for its forms/symbols (counting down) — provide the function and note it.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()
import re, sys
s = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
m = {}
def rep(mo):
    g = mo.group(0)
    if g not in m:
        m[g] = "GUID-%d" % (len(m)+1)
    return m[g]
s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
sys.stdout.write(s)
import json, re, sys
langs = ['en','pt','es','sv','cs','fr','nl','de','it']
out = ['//! The default contents of a new project in each language: what `new` makes, with',
       '//! `@G<n>` standing for a GUID made fresh for each project.',
       '']
for l in langs:
    s = open(f'/tmp/tpl/{l}.bimcraft').read()
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": 0', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m:
            m[g] = '@G%d' % len(m)
        return m[g]
    s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
    d = json.loads(s)
    mini = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(',',':'))
    assert '"#' not in mini
    out.append(f'pub const {l.upper()}: &str = r##"{mini}"##;')
open('/workspace/src/templates.rs','w').write('\n'.join(out)+'\n')

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()
import re, sys
s = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
m = {}
def rep(mo):
    g = mo.group(0)
    if g not in m:
        m[g] = "GUID-%d" % (len(m)+1)
    return m[g]
s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
sys.stdout.write(s)
import json, re, sys
langs = ['en','pt','es','sv','cs','fr','nl','de','it']
out = ['//! The default contents of a new project in each language: what `new` makes, with',
       '//! `@G<n>` standing for a GUID made fresh for each project.',
       '']
for l in langs:
    s = open(f'/tmp/tpl/{l}.bimcraft').read()
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": 0', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m:
            m[g] = '@G%d' % len(m)
        return m[g]
    s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
    d = json.loads(s)
    mini = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(',',':'))
    assert '"#' not in mini
    out.append(f'pub const {l.upper()}: &str = r##"{mini}"##;')
open('/workspace/src/templates.rs','w').write('\n'.join(out)+'\n')

| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) 
after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its 
own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer 
walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from 
the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's 
Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are 
subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a 
path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its 
level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen 
from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project 
parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água 
fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's 
language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an 
elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an 
`IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the 
luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and 
`IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 
127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |
| Lightning protection (SPDA) | Air terminals (captores), down conductors (condutores de descida), earthing electrodes (hastes de aterramento), inspection boxes and earthing conductors (the ring or mesh), the vocabulary of NBR 5419; Revit has no such tab, so its tools are BIMCraft's own, on the same runs and fixtures. A down conductor is a run that stands upright down a wall (the same point twice 
and two heights), round in steel or copper or a flat strip; an earthing conductor runs under the level; both belong to a named system. The project starts with a Franklin air terminal in three heights, an earthing rod driven 2.4 or 3 m and a round inspection box, original drawings in the project's language. IFC4 has no lightning protection, so the terminals, rods and boxes are 
`IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` and `InspectionBox`, which a reader can filter on and BIMCraft reads back into a family of its category; the conductors are `IfcCableSegment` `CONDUCTORSEGMENT`, told apart by a `Category` BIMCraft writes. A conductor under the level shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth) |
| Data (lógica, dados e voz) | Data outlets, voice outlets, racks, patch panels, the cable trays of the Electrical tab and structured cabling, the vocabulary of NBR 14565. Cabling is a run like a wire, round, in a named `system` (a link, a network), a Cat6, a Cat6A or an optical cable to start from. The project starts with a data and a voice outlet (a plate with its jacks cut in), a patch panel 
and a floor rack in three sizes, each at the height its type says, original drawings in the project's language, written as `IfcOutlet` (`DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`), `IfcCommunicationsAppliance` (`NETWORKAPPLIANCE`) and, for the rack, which IFC4 has no class for, an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `Rack`, and read back into a family of the same category (an `IfcOutlet` of another 
type is read as a power outlet) |
| Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 
kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands 
as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category. `reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and 
anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end 
to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project, which `reinforce` takes with 
`preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on 
it. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and 
a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a section's cut seen through the concrete. |
| Types | Wall, floor, ceiling, door, window, column, structural column, footing, beam, strip footing, pipe, conduit, cable tray, wire, down conductor, earthing conductor, cable, roof and railing types; editing one changes every element that uses it (a run type's roundness and material too) |
| Materials | A library of materials in each project, as Revit's Material Browser: each with a shading colour, a cut pattern and a surface pattern (solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete or insulation), drawn in code. Wall, floor, roof and ceiling types are built of layers, each a function, a material from the library and a thickness of its own, adding up to the 
type's: a wall's from the exterior in, the others' from the top down. Plans and sections cut each layer and hatch it with its material's cut pattern where it's wide enough to hold it (a drafting pattern, the same on screen and on paper); a floor's top in plan and a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan show their surface pattern at its size in the building; the 3D view shades each layer in its 
material's colour. A material may have a texture over its colour in the 3D view: a pattern drawn in code (brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof tiles, fabric, metal or insulation, each at its real size) or a picture you add (a PNG or a JPEG, kept in the project, at most 1024 px a side, up to 24 of them), laid on every face of what's made of the material at the size you give it, 
turned and moved as you say, by the face's own axes (across a wall, a slab's east and north); the library's materials come with theirs. Paint (PT) lays a material, with its texture, over one face of an element, a wall's exterior or a floor's top, over what its type is made of, as Revit's Paint does. A material, with its picture, can be kept in your Favorites, a file of your own (`favorites.json` 
in your configuration folder, or where `BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES` says) that every project reads; textures show in the 3D view alone (plans and sections keep their patterns), and IFC carries the colour |
| Editing | Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is); move, copy, rotate and mirror, with the walls joined to them stretching to stay joined and doors and windows going with their walls (a mirrored wall runs back the other way, its exterior mirrored); trim or extend two walls to a corner; split a wall, an arc into two arcs; flip 
walls; delete (a wall takes its doors and windows with it, and they their tags; a roof or floor walls are attached to lets them go); undo and redo |

Construction, whatever their names; a rule that names a phase, an option or a set follows it when it is renamed or combined); the desktop's Demolish tool (DW) takes an element down in the phase of the view it is clicked in, and a second click takes it back; templates can control a view's phase and its options; sheets print each view in its phase; a project's phases, filters, overrides and sets 
are saved with it. A project saved before phases that holds a project parameter named `Phase Created`, `Phase Demolished` or `Design Option` opens with it renamed (`Phase Created Parameter`), its values with it |
| Sheets | ISO A0 to A4, landscape, with a title block (project, sheet name and number, scale); plans, sections, elevations and the 3D view placed on them at a scale and titled, schedules as ruled tables, text notes on the paper, a view on one sheet; PNG, and PDF: one sheet, or every sheet a page |
| Schedules | Schedule views of rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, down conductors, earthing conductors, cables, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, as Revit's Schedule/Quantities makes them: the fields chosen and ordered from the category's own (Area, Width, 
Count…), the project parameters for it and, for components, their families' parameters; calculated fields, formulas over the row's other fields as a family's are (`Area * 120`, `Perimeter * Finish Height / 1e6`); filters (equals, greater than, contains, begins with, has a value…) that every row holds to, comparing values as the schedule shows them; sorting by fields in turn, ascending or 
descending (the phase fields in the project's order of phases, not by name), and grouped, a row for each set of their values, its count and totals summed; totals under the rows. Every project has a Room, Door, Window, Wall, Floor and Level Schedule, each the project's own once changed; CSV; on sheets, totals and all |
| Project parameters | Values of your own that each element of their categories holds (text, numbers, lengths, yes or no, unset a no), as Revit's project parameters are: set in Properties or with `modify`, shown, filtered and sorted in schedules and read by their formulas, and written to IFC in a `Project Parameters` property set and read back from it; renamed, schedules follow; taken off a 
category, its elements and schedules lose them |
| Units | Lengths shown and typed in millimetres, centimetres, metres, fractional inches, decimal feet, or feet and fractional inches (to 1/16"), areas in m² or ft², in drawings, schedules and the desktop alike; a length typed with its own unit (`10' 6 1/2"`, `3 m`) reads as that. The model, files and every command keep millimetres |
| Languages | English, Brazilian Portuguese, Spanish, Czech, French, German, Dutch or Italian for the desktop; those languages or Swedish for each project (and Vietnamese, Simplified or Traditional Chinese for the desktop alone, Chinese drawn with a Chinese font the system has: a drawing's lettering has no hanzi): a project's language names what commands make (levels, sections, elevations, rooms, 
schedules) and is what its drawings print (SOBE, SUBE, UPP or AUF on stairs, ESCALA, SKALA or MASSSTAB in the title block, schedule headings); what's already named stays. Commands' messages stay English, for agents |
| Families | BIMCraft's own parametric components, never Autodesk's `.rfa`: a family has parameters (lengths, numbers, angles, yes or no, materials; each type's, or each component's), types that set them, and forms, each a profile drawn in its own axes and swept across them, every size a number or a formula as Revit's are (`Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`), each form of a material, there 
while a yes/no parameter or a formula says. A new project comes with ten of them (tables, chairs, beds, sofas, desks, wardrobes, base cabinets, WCs, washbasins, bathtubs), named and worded in its language; more load from .json files. A component places a family's type at a point, turned and mirrored, its instance parameters its own; plans show it from above, the parts under a higher one hidden (a 
table's legs under its top), and sections and elevations beyond their line, never cut, as Revit shows furniture; the 3D view shades each form in its material's colour, textured as its material is. A form may be turned about an axis in its plane (a pipe, a bowl, a shade: `axis`, and `from` and `to` in degrees, up to a full turn), and a `void` form cuts the solid forms listed before it that it 
passes through (a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, a sash round its pane), exactly: a solid cut by a solid, in any shape. The Family Editor in the desktop edits a family's parameters, types, forms and symbols as text, shows it on a preview you can turn, and makes it the project's, saves it to a `.json` file, or keeps it, with the materials it's made of, in the Favorites |
| IFC import | IFC2x3 and IFC4 files, as Revit and other BIM tools write them: storeys, straight and curved walls with their doors and windows (cut to a roof over them, attached to it), floors level or sloped and ceilings, with the holes in them, rooms, columns (structural ones, which carry load, in their own category), beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, conductors and 
cables (runs, found as the longest direction a body spreads in and the section square to it, or, when the body is one profile extruded along anything but up, that way, so a beam shorter than it is deep is still a beam; an upright one running up, with the justification and the `IfcSystem` BIMCraft wrote), isolated footings, structural floors, grids, stairs and ramps of straight flights with the 
landings between them (a landing slab on its own is a floor), railings (by their axis, or a straight one by its body), roofs flat, sloping all round over any footprint with gable ends, courtyards and openings through them, or one profile swept across, masses (proxies of object type `Mass`, a lofted one with its `BIMCraft_Mass` property set), and the openings through floors, ceilings and roofs (as

207 sm.txt
# Structure and the discipline tabs (Plumbing, Electrical, SPDA, Data)

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Structure (`runs.rs`, `structure.rs`; the design for the five discipline tabs is in [docs/disciplines.md](../disciplines.md)). A run
(`model::Run`) is a straight element from `start` to `end` in plan; its `offset` mm over its level is the height of its `justify` line
(top, centre or bottom) at the start, `end_offset` at the end (level when none), `system` the name of the system it is in: a beam, a
strip footing, a pipe (Plumbing), and what the other tabs draw (conduits, cable trays, down conductors, data cabling) as further
`Element` variants over the same struct, as `Door` and `Window` share `Opening`; `model::run_arm!` is the pattern for any of them, so a
place that treats runs alike names no category, and a new category is a line there. Its type is `Types::runs[category][name]`, a `RunType`
(`width` across by `depth` deep, or round, in a `material` of the library). The section is square to the axis, so a sloped run is
`depth / cos θ` deep vertically (`Geom::half`). `runs::Geom` is the one place that knows the geometry (centre line, `footprint`,
`prism` for a rectangle, `tube` for a round one, `z_span`); plans, sections (a prism is cut like any solid; a tube by the plane
through the section's line, `Solid::cuts`: the hull of where its edges cross it, a ring, an ellipse when oblique), 3D, snaps and IFC call
it and know no category. A run's heights are those of its `justify` line, which a beam or a footing has at the top by default and
anything else at the middle (`runs::default_justify`); the desktop keeps each run tool's own justification and offset
(`keep_run_options`). A beam or strip footing can't stand or lean past 75°
(`runs::check`, `may_stand`: what stands is a column; a pipe, a conduit or a conductor may stand, a riser). In plan (`render::stands`) a footing or a run
hangs under the level it is drawn on, its top flush with the view's bottom, and is seen (`seen_below` allows `TOL` for these only,
or a wall of the storey below would show in the plan above); through the cut plane it's cut; over it and under the view range's top
it's dashed; a faint dashed centre line is drawn where it's seen or overhead, which is also where a click picks it. A structural column and an
isolated footing are `Column`s in their own categories (`Element::StructuralColumn`, `Element::Footing`; ask `Element::column()`,
`Model::column_type(e)` and `column_outline(e)`, which take the element, not the column) with types of their own
(`Types::structural_column`, `Types::footing`); a footing is laid down, its `height` its thickness and its `base_offset` putting its
top at the level (the command's `thickness` and `offset`). A floor is `structural` or not, the one flag, and its schedule and IFC say it.
`runs_of` and `stood_of` build what a command would make, so a tool's sketch is the element its click makes. The desktop's
`Tool::Run(category, start)` and `Tool::Stand(category)` serve every category: a tab adds a ribbon button and its rows in
`structure.rs`, `properties.rs` and `lang.rs`, not a tool. The Floor tool makes structural floors while `floor_structural` is set (SB,
the Structure tab's button; every other `set_tool` clears it); CL is the structural column on the Structure tab and the architectural one
elsewhere, as in Revit. IFC writes a run as an extrusion along its own axis (`Step::body_along`, `aim`) of the class and predefined type
the one table `runs::IFC` gives its category (import reads the same table back, `runs::from_ifc`), each structural element with
`LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, a run's system as an `IfcSystem` (named for it, its GlobalIds following the name) the runs in it
are assigned to by an `IfcRelAssignsToGroup`, its `Justification` and `Category` in `BIMCraft_Run`, and its material as an `IfcMaterial`. A beam, a column, a structural column and a
pad footing carry their section on their type, the IFC4 way (`Step::typed_member`, `write_types`): the `IfcBeamType`, `IfcColumnType` or
`IfcFootingType` is related by `IfcRelAssociatesMaterial` to an `IfcMaterialProfileSet` of one `IfcMaterialProfile`, holding the type's
material (a beam type's; a column type has none, so the material is `$`) and its profile, an `IfcRectangleProfileDef` of the width by the
depth or an `IfcCircleProfileDef` of half the width, in millimetres as every length is. Each occurrence is related to an
`IfcMaterialProfileSetUsage` of that set (one for each cardinal point, shared by the occurrences placed by it): a beam's cardinal point is
the line its heights are on, the top (8), the middle (5) or the bottom (2) of its section, a column's and a footing's the middle (5). The
beam has no other material association, so the importer reads a run's material through the usage (`element_material`). The profile
definition (`Step::section_profile`, keyed by `Section`) is written once for a section, and the type's profile and its occurrences' bodies
share it; two types of one name and two sections (a column's and a structural column's) are two type objects. A strip footing, a pipe and
the other runs have no profile set, only the plain material.
Import (`import::run_in`) finds a run's axis as the direction its body's points spread furthest in (power iteration on their
covariance), so a beam rolled about its axis comes in as the box round it; an axis that stands (a riser) has its width along east and
runs up; the justification BIMCraft wrote puts the heights back on the line they were typed at (`Geom::half`), none meaning the middle;
a system comes from the IfcSystem the product is assigned to, and its category from the class and type, or BIMCraft's `Category`
where a class has several; `LoadBearing` makes a column or a floor structural.

**Sizing** is a command with no model behind it, so it needs no connectors: `circuit` (`nbr5410.rs`, its tables in `nbr5410/tables.rs` as NBR 5410:2004 prints them: Tabelas 36 and 37 current capacity for methods A1 to D, 40 and 41 temperature and soil, 42 and 45 grouping, 47, 48 and 58) sizes one 
electrical circuit for copper: the design current from watts or VA, the demand and power factors and the phases at the voltage `system` it is given (it reads nothing from the model), then the smallest section and breaker with I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the 
breakers of NBR NM 60898) and a voltage drop within the limit (4 %, from the conductor's resistance at its working temperature and 0.1 ohm/km), with the neutral and the protective conductor. A section or breaker already chosen is never made smaller. It does not check aluminium, trays (methods E and 
F), several layers, short circuit, harmonics or the conditions of a reduced neutral, and says so; a circuit in the model and a panel schedule come after it. `conduit_fill` (`conduit.rs`, its catalogues in `conduit/tables.rs`) checks a conduit's fill: the conductors of a circuit (phases, neutral, 
protective; by outside diameter) over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two and 40 % for three or more (NBR 5410), and the smallest size of a family that takes them. The dimensions are the makers' own (Amanco Wavin PVC, Elecon steel, Corfio flexible cable), each family 
naming its document, page and address; the inside diameter is derived (outside less twice the wall); a cable the catalogue lacks (EPR, above 240 mm²) leaves the fill pending, never guessed. Trays are not sized. `drain_size` and `vent_size` (`drainage.rs`) size sanitary drains and vents as NBR 8160 
asks, by the fixture units (UHC) they carry, with the standard's own tables: Tabela 3 (the units and smallest drain of each fixture), 5 (branches), 7 (building drains and collectors by slope), 6 (stacks by the building's floors), 8 (branch vents), 2 (vent stacks and headers by the DN served, its 
units and the longest length of each vent DN) and 1 (a trap's longest run to its vent). A drain is never smaller than its fixtures' own drains or than one flowing into it (`min_dn`), and a building drain is DN 100 at least. They are stateless, so none of this needs a pipe network; a network that 
carries the units along the runs comes with connectors. `storm_size` (`storm.rs`) sizes storm drains as NBR 10844 asks: the flow Q = I·A/60 from a rainfall and a roof area, a downpipe by the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses (read curve by curve: the water depth in the gutter, the 
downpipe's length and a sharp-edged or funnel outlet; 70 mm inside at least; off the chart nothing is read) and a horizontal drain by Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, which reproduces its Table 4 within 1 %; 0.5 % slope at least). `water_size` (`water.rs`) sizes a cold water pipe of PVC 
soldável as NBR 5626 asks: the design flow of the fixtures by the method the project chooses (weights, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, or every fixture at once), the smallest DN within 3 m/s, the Darcy-Weisbach head loss over the length and the equivalent length of the fittings, and the pressure left (10 kPa at 
least at a point of use). `hydrant_size` (`hydrant.rs`) sizes hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks: the system type and fire reserve of Tabela 3 by occupation column and built area, the flow of the two most unfavourable jets of Tabela 2's type, and a pipe's speed (5 m/s at 
most), Hazen-Williams head loss (Tabela 1) and the head needed at its start. `load_points` (`loads.rs`) lists what a dwelling's rooms must have as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks: one ceiling lighting point per room (100 VA up to 6 m², 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above) and the general-use 
outlets by the room's kind, which its name says or `kind` gives (a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area and laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room and bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and by perimeter above), with their power (600 VA each for the first 3 
points of a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry and 100 VA after, or for the first 2 by the alternative where those rooms have more than 6 points together; 100 VA a point elsewhere) on the points a room has. It reads the model's rooms (inside the walls' finish) or the rooms it is 
given, and changes nothing. It leaves out the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, where the outlets stand, and the TUE, and says so.

**Electrical settings** (`electrical.rs`) are the tables circuits, panels and connectors will name, as Revit's Electrical Settings: `Voltage` (`nominal`, and the band `min` to `max` a device may read within), `DistributionSystem` (`phases` 1 to 3, `wires` the line conductors and the neutral and not 
the protective one, and the voltages it supplies by name: `l_l` between lines, `l_n` to the neutral, `l_g` to earth, and `ground`, how it is earthed as IEC 60364-1 names it) and `WireType` (`material`, `temperature`, `insulation`, a `note` saying where the ampacities come from, and `sizes`, a row 
for each section with its `ampacity`). Every section is in mm² whatever the project's units; a size a standard gives in AWG or kcmil is converted and keeps its name as `label`. Each is a map of `Model` (`voltages`, `distribution_systems`, `wire_types`), a library entry (`Kind::Voltage`, 
`Kind::DistributionSystem`, `Kind::WireType`, so each has an id and a GUID, comes in with Insert from File and is renamed with `rename_entry`), and has a command that makes, edits, renames and deletes it and, without a `name`, lists it (`voltage`, `distribution_system`, `wire_type`); `inspect` 
lists all three. A system names voltages, so `Model::lib_refs_mut` hands them out (a file holds their GUIDs, a rename follows) and `Model::check` refuses a system that names one the project lacks, saying which and listing the ones it has, and `voltage` refuses to delete one a system supplies; with 
three phases `l_l` must be about root three times `l_n`. `Model::voltage_range`, `system_voltages` and `wire_ampacity` are what circuits will ask: the band of a voltage, the voltages a system supplies (the ones a circuit on it may have) and the ampacity of a section in a wire type's table. A new 
project starts with `data/electrical.json`, data and not code: 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of NBR 5410:2004 Tabelas 36 and 37 (PVC 70 °C and XLPE or EPR 90 °C, seeded from `nbr5410/tables.rs`: method B1, two loaded conductors, a test keeps them equal) and of 
NFPA 70 Table 310.16 (THHN 90 °C, THW 75 °C); their ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked, and one number for a section cannot say how a wire is laid, so a wire type's `note` says. `start_system` and `start_wire` name the ones a new panel or circuit starts with for the project's units 
(Europe's in metric, North America's in feet and inches). None of it goes to IFC: the tables are project data, and what they produce (voltage, current, section) will go in the device's property set once circuits exist. On the desktop, Manage > Electrical Settings (`ui-egui/src/electrical.rs`) is 
one dialog with a tab for each table: rows to add and delete, a voltage chosen from the project's own for each line of a system, and a wire type's table of sections below its fields. It is a draft, applied by OK or Apply as one undo step (`Session::transaction`) through the three commands, in an 
order the core accepts (`renames::plan`, which the other Manage dialogs use, orders each table's renames and deletes; the voltages are made before the systems that name them and taken away after the systems that no longer do). A system's voltages are held by their rows' keys, so one renamed in the 
dialog is still the one named. A blank or repeated name, a voltage a system supplies being deleted, and what the core refuses are said inside the dialog, which stays open. Not yet: circuits, panels and the load schedule, connectors in families.

The discipline tabs after Structure add data to this, no engine code of their own. Plumbing: `pipe` (PI), types in PVC and copper
(`Types::runs["pipe"]`, outside diameters, so a pipe's `width` is its diameter and its schedule says Diameter). Electrical: `conduit`
(CN), `duct` (DU: a rectangular or round duct, written as `IfcDuctSegment`; only a Revit import makes them in practice) `cabletray` (CT, `cable_tray`: the one rectangular run) and `wire` (EW), by their outside size. Lightning protection (NBR 5419):
`downconductor` (DC, may stand: a riser down a wall) and `groundconductor` (GC), two runs of one IFC class that `BIMCraft_Run`'s `Category`
tells apart; an air terminal, an earthing electrode and an inspection box are components of their own family categories, written as
`IfcBuildingElementProxy` of the object type `Category::ifc` names, so the product's name (not its object type) holds `Family:Type` and
import reads it from there. Data (NBR 14565): `cable` (CB, `cabling`), a run like a wire, so a file's `IfcCableSegment` is a wire unless its
`Category` says cable; data and voice outlets (`IfcOutlet` `DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`; one of no type reads as the power outlet,
`Category::from_ifc` taking the first of equals), a patch panel (`IfcCommunicationsAppliance`) and a rack (a proxy of object type `Rack`);
the Cable Tray tool is the Electrical tab's, on the Data tab too. A fixture or a
device is a component of a family whose `family::Category` says what it is (a sanitary fixture, a floor drain, a pipe fitting, a pipe
accessory…); `Category::ifc` is its IFC class, predefined type and, where IFC has no class (lightning protection), the object type a
proxy carries, and `Category::from_ifc` reads the same table back, so a category is one row, in `family.rs`. A family's `kind`
(`Category::kinds`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`… for a sanitary fixture, `floor_drain`… for a drain, `bend`, `tee`… for a fitting, the names the
sizing commands count fixtures by) says which one it is, and `Family::ifc` writes that kind's predefined type in place of the
category's `.NOTDEFINED.`; the import reads it back with `Category::kind_of`, the first kind of a predefined type two share. The starter families are
`fixtures.rs` (original forms, named in the project's language; a fitting or a valve is centred on its pipe, along x, so placing it at the
pipe's height lines them up; a wall device, a board and a luminaire carry their `Mounting Height` in their type, so the Fixture tool
places them at the level and they stand where they hang). The desktop's `mep.rs` has one tool for every fixture and device, `Tool::Fixture(key)`: the families of the
kinds its `FixtureTool` names, listed in its Type Selector and placed as the Component tool places them (`placing` takes the tool's
kinds), and the tabs' ribbon panels; a fixture's two-letter shortcut is in `mep::FIXTURES`, not `SHORTCUTS`, since no command makes
one. Edit Type of a run type also sets whether it is round (a diameter, no depth) and its material.

Reinforcement (`rebar.rs`, `model::Rebar`, `Element::Rebar`, category `rebar`, the `rebar` command; tests in `rebar_tests.rs`). A bar is one
element: a round bar of `diameter` mm (3 to 100) bent along `path` (points in mm, `z` over its level), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless
told), with the `host` it reinforces (a beam, a column, a footing or a floor, held as a `Guid`, and it goes when its host does). A hoop
is a bar whose last point is its first; a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam, is one command with `count` and `step`, which makes one
element for each (IFC has one `IfcReinforcingBar` for each, and a bar schedule counts them). It has no type: the diameter and the grade
are its own, and the bends are sharp, with no hooks, so its length is the sum of its pieces (`rebar::length`) and its weight that
length of steel at 7850 kg/m³ (`rebar::weight_kg`). Nothing checks that it lies inside its host: `reinforce` places bars inside by construction. The schedule of category `rebar` lists Id, Level, Grade, Diameter,
Length, Count, Weight and Host, and grouped by Grade, Diameter and Length with Count and Weight totalled it is a bar schedule. IFC
writes each as an `IfcReinforcingBar` (`SteelGrade`, `NominalDiameter`, `CrossSectionArea`, `BarLength`) with a body of an
`IfcSweptDiskSolid` along an `IfcPolyline`, aggregated (`IfcRelAggregates`) to its host, or contained in its storey when it has none;
import reads the same back, with the host found by the aggregation. The 3D view draws a tube along each straight piece
(`rebar::tubes`, built with a round run's tube), which the concrete round a bar hides: look at bars with their host hidden. A section draws each bar it cuts as a
dot over the host's poché (`render::section_in` keeps them out of the host's pieces, which would swallow them); a plan draws them too (`render::bar_in_plan`).

Importing a structural program's IFC (Eberick, Cype and the like; tests in `eberick_tests.rs`, written by hand, never from anyone's project). Each
product is named by its mark, so a name that is not its type's (BIMCraft names a product by its type, and writes it as its object type too) is its
`Mark` parameter, for the categories in `import::MARKED` (beams, columns, structural columns, footings, strip footings and floors; not stairs,
which BIMCraft calls "Stair"). The single values of every property set that is not BIMCraft's (`BIMCraft_*`, `RoomSeparation`; `Project Parameters`
is read by its names as written) are project parameters named for the property, a character a formula can't say turned into a space
(`parameter_name`: "Cargas de parede (G2)" is "Cargas de parede G2"), lengths in the file's unit made millimetres; `LoadBearing` is left out because
it already makes a column or a floor structural. The cover Eberick sets (`Cobrimento`, `ConcreteCover`) is therefore on the host as a length, for the
rules that will arm it. A run is found in its body as the way it spreads furthest, except where the body is one extruded profile and the extrusion is
not up: then it runs along the extrusion (`Reader::extrusion`), because a beam between two columns can be shallower than it is deep, and its body then
spreads furthest up. A strip footing, a plan outline stood up, is still read by its shape. A landing slab that belongs to no stair is a floor.

Bars by rules (`reinforce.rs`, the `reinforce` command; tests in `reinforce_tests.rs`). The engineer says how many bars, how thick and how far
apart; the module lays them out in the host's own frame (`Frame`: along, across, up) inside the cover and checks that what is asked fits, with the
message saying what to change. It holds geometry and no standard's table: a spacing or a count is never decided here (that is design), and the
clearance between bars (`clearance`, their thickness and at least 20 mm unless told) is the only rule it brings. Parameters are read with serde types
that deny unknown fields (`Row`, `Pitch`, `Stirrup`, `ColumnBars`, `Mesh`, `Grid`), by key, so a key that is not the host's is refused with the host named.
The cover is `{top, bottom, sides}` (Revit's faces: the top and bottom faces of a beam, a footing or a floor, the ends of a column, and all round
the rest) or one number, and where none is given the host's `Cobrimento` or `ConcreteCover` parameter (a length in mm, as the import of an Eberick IFC
leaves it) is the cover. A spacing is the most between bars: `spread` and `stations` place them evenly from end to end, so the count follows the length
(Revit's Maximum Spacing) and `ends` gives closer stirrups in the first and last `length` mm. A stirrup is a closed loop; with `hook` it runs on past
its first corner to a tail turned into the section at each end (`stirrup`). A beam has `bottom` and `top` rows, `stirrup`, `skin` and `anchor`; a
column `bars` (`x` and `y` along each face, corners counted; a round one, `count` round its circle), `stirrup` (a round one's a polygon of 24 sides), `ties`
(across a rectangular section; with `hook` a tail at each end turned toward the other axis) and `anchor`; a footing a `mesh` of two layers with `hook`
turning their ends up (a round one's bars stop at its circle, `half` in `footing`); a floor `bottom` and `top` meshes (`hook` turning their ends up from the
bottom one and down from the top one, square to the slab's top) whose bars stop a cover short of its outline and of its
openings (`chords`, a scan line through the outline and the openings together; a bar parallel to an opening's edge and nearer it than the cover keeps
its cover from the ends only). A sloped floor's layers are measured from its top face, square to it (`off`, and its secant for the height plumb), so the
cover and the thickness are the type's and its bars follow the slope; a mesh on a slope is one plane's bars. Round beams and strip footings are refused. Each bar is a `rebar` element of the host with a `layer`
(`bottom`, `top`, `skin`, `stirrup`, `bars`, `tie`, `mesh x`, `mesh y`, `bottom x`, `top y`, ...); reinforcing a host again replaces its bars that have a layer
and leaves the ones with none, which were drawn by hand, and one command makes up to `rebar::MAX_BARS`. A bar's layer is in the project file and the
schedule (a field a bar schedule may show), not in IFC. What it does not do: bends other than a hook, laps and splices, bars of a round beam, and any check
against a standard. A section shows a bar in its plane as a strip along it and one it crosses as a dot (the cut of the bar's tube, `section_in`); a bar
beyond the cut stays hidden by the concrete it is in.

content.content:
More of `reinforce`. `hosts` arms a list (`rebar::MAX_HOSTS`, 1000) alike in one command: every host's bars are made before any is replaced, so one that refuses (its refusal names its category and id) arms none, and `rebar::MAX_BARS_ALL` (20000) caps all of them
together. A `hook` on a beam's `bottom` and `top` rows is the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at each end
(a number for both, or `{start, end}`), and on a column's `bars` a leg turned into the section along the way across the face the bar is on
(`{below, above}`); `legs` reads it, with its own words when it is not a length, and a leg that does not stay inside the stirrup (a column's: stop
short of the middle) is refused. The bends are sharp, as every bar's are, and each leg is a piece of the path, so the length and the weight count it.
A `reinforcement_preset` is `reinforce::Preset`, a kind of host (`KINDS`) and the parameters that kind takes, in `Model::reinforcement` and as a library
entry (`Kind::ReinforcementPreset`, so it has an id and a GUID, comes in with Insert from File and is renamed with `rename_entry`); it is checked
for its keys and its size when saved (`Preset::check`, `MAX_PRESETS`) and against a host only when it arms one. `reinforce` with `preset` takes its parameters
and lets any given with it replace them, key by key; a preset of another kind than the host is refused, saying both. Plans: a bar of the plan's level
is drawn from above, solid when the cut plane is over its lowest point and dashed when it is over the plane and under the view range's top, a bar
that stands (a column's) as a dot, and bars that lie on one another (a column's stirrups, one over the next) once.

Bends beyond a hook. `bottom.bent` `{count, angle?, top?}` (`Bent`, `bent_up`) takes `count` of a beam's inner bottom bars (the two at the corners hold the
stirrups and stay straight; the others are picked evenly) and bends them up at each end: along the top face for `top` mm from the end (a fifth of the
length unless told), down a slope of `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) to the bottom row's level and along it. They are on the layer `bent`,
have no hook, count as bottom steel in the check, and are refused where the slopes meet in the middle, where the section is too shallow to rise
in, and where one comes within the clearance of a top bar at the top. `bars.jog` `{by, from_top, slope?}` (`Jog`, `step`, `stepped`) steps a column's
bars `by` mm toward the axis (a corner bar along both faces, a face bar across its own, a round column's radially), the step starting `from_top` mm below
the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told); the points of the bar above the step move with it, including a hook's leg, and
the bars at their new places are checked against one another for the clearance.

The check (`reinforce/norm.rs`). `check` `"NBR 6118"`, with `aggressiveness` (1 to 4) and `fck` (MPa), makes `reinforce` return `notes`: where the bars
made fall short of the usual limits for the kind of host (Table 7.2's cover by class; for a beam the 4 % most, the 0.15 % least up to C30, skin bars over 600 mm
deep, stirrups of 5 mm to a tenth of the width at most min(0.6 d, 300) apart; for a column bars of 10 mm to an eighth of the side, 4 bars or 6 round,
centres at most min(2 sides, 400), 0.4 to 8 % of steel, stirrups of 5 mm or a quarter of the bars' at most min(200, the side, 12 bars) apart; for a floor
bars of at most an eighth of the thickness at most min(2 h, 200) apart). A note never refuses: an engineer may know better, and the bars are made.
It reads only the bars made, so a limit that needs shear, the load or the aggregate is not in it. The numbers are typed from handbooks and course material
that print them, not from the standard's text, which is paid for, and the item numbers are the 2014 edition's at the level of the chapter's item: check
one against a copy before relying on it. The desktop's Check row (Standard, Aggressiveness class, fck) shows the notes inside the dialog, which stays
open, with the bars made, so a field can change and OK remake them.

The Reinforce dialog (`crates/ui-egui/src/reinforce.rs`, Structure > Reinforcement, RF; tests in `tests/reinforce.rs`). It opens on the one beam, column,
structural column, footing or floor selected (anything else says what to select), with the form of its kind (`BEAM`, `COLUMN`, `FOOTING`, `FLOOR`: tables of
groups of fields, each field the path of the parameter it sets, such as `bottom.count`). Every field is text: a count is a whole number, a bar size is mm,
a length is read in the project's units (`Units::parse`); a field left empty is not sent, a group with none filled is left out, and the command is the one
that says what is missing. OK builds the parameters and runs `reinforce` as one undo step; a refusal is the command's own words, shown inside the dialog
(a status box in the view's corner could lie over its buttons) with the dialog left open and the project unchanged, and a field that is not a number is
named before the command is asked. It takes any number of elements selected, of one form (a mixed selection says so), and arms them with one `hosts` command; Remove Bars removes the bars of all. What was typed is kept for the next element of the same form (not in the project, not on disk). The 
Preset row lists the project's presets of the form: choosing one fills the fields (`ReinforceDialog::load`, the reverse of `params`, lengths in the project's units), Save Preset keeps the fields as they are under the name typed (`reinforcement_preset`, the parameters without the hosts), and Delete 
Preset takes the chosen one away; each keeps the dialog open. Remove Bars, shown
when the element has bars the command made (those with a layer), deletes them and leaves the ones drawn by hand. The fields' accessible names are
"Group: Field" (`Bottom bars: Count`), and the cover's is `Cover`, its label having a colon so that no two nodes carry the name.

**Connectors.** A family's `connectors` (`family::Connector`, a list for any discipline; today the electrical device's) say what
a placed device draws: `kind` `power` or `switch`, `system` `power-balanced`, `power-unbalanced` or `switch`, `poles` (1 to 3),
`voltage`, `load_va`, `power_factor` and a `classification`. The numbers are numbers or formulas over the family's parameters, so a
type sets its load (the starter luminaires' `Load` parameter) and an instance parameter lets one component set its own; a
`power-unbalanced` connector's `load_va` may be a list, one load for each pole, and a single number is shared out evenly.
`Family::check` refuses a family of two `power` connectors, a kind and system that don't go together, poles, voltage, power factor
or load out of range for any type, and a load on a switch. A connector is a part (`HasPart`: an id and a GUID, kept by place
while the family is edited), and a family without any reads and places as it always did. A component's `element_json` carries
`connectors` worked out for its type (`Family::connector_values`: `load_va` in all, `load_va_by_phase`), which a circuit will sum;
there are no circuits, panels or fitting-to-pipe joins yet, and the connector holds no position. `Model::warnings` (shown by
`inspect`; `Model::check` stays an error only) says which lighting, outlet or switch family in use holds no connector, so its devices
count as zero load. IFC writes each device with a connector `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` (`NumberOfPoles`, and for a power
connector `PowerFactor` and `RatedVoltage`) and `BIMCraft_Connector` (`System`, `Classification`, `LoadVA`, `LoadVAPhase1`…); IFC
import doesn't read them back.
